summary: Describes problems that arise when a device is connected to several networks at once and receives configuration from each. Some settings apply to the whole device and others to one interface, so conflicts can cause traffic to use the wrong interface or names to clash. It is a problem statement, not a solution.

plainLanguage.summary: When a laptop is on WiFi and a VPN at the same time, each network sends it settings: an address, a gateway, a list of DNS servers. Some of those settings fit one network only, but the computer keeps them in a single global list. This RFC describes what goes wrong as a result and what choices a device has to make.

questions: why does my device pick the wrong network interface
why does my device pick the wrong network
subtitle: What goes wrong when a device is attached to several networks at once and each of them hands it settings.

tldr.problem: A device on several networks at once receives settings from each of them, but most implementations keep those settings as a single global list instead of one list per network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a multiple-interface node, then lists the failures that follow: names that will not resolve, packets that leave by the wrong interface, source addresses that are invalid for the network they are used on, and policies from different actors that contradict each other.
tldr.outcome: It is a problem statement rather than a solution. The RFC groups the causes into five categories and leaves the remedy to a later requirements document.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A multihomed node may have multiple provisioning domains, reached through physical or virtual interfaces. A node may be simultaneously connected to a wired Ethernet LAN, an 802.11 LAN, a 3G cell network, one or multiple VPN connections, or one or multiple tunnels, automatic or manual. Current laptops and smartphones typically have multiple access network interfaces and are thus often connected to different provisioning domains at the same time.

The node receives configuration information from each of its attached networks through various mechanisms such as DHCPv4, DHCPv6, PPP and IPv6 Router Advertisements. Some received configuration objects are specific to an interface, such as the IP address and the link prefix. Others are typically considered by implementations as being global to the node, called node-scoped in this document, such as the routing information including the default gateway, DNS server IP addresses and address selection policies.

When the received node-scoped configuration objects have different values from each other in different provisioning domains, such as different DNS server IP addresses, different default gateways or different address selection policies, the node has to decide which one to use or how it will merge them. Other issues result from simultaneous attachment to multiple networks, such as addressing and naming space overlaps, regardless of the provisioning mechanism. The document defines the multiple interfaces (MIF) node and the scope of the work, describes related work, lists the issues and then summarises the underlying problems. It is a problem statement, not a solution; the companion document RFC 6419 discusses current practices in various implementations dealing with MIF.
sections.plainLanguage: When a laptop is on WiFi and a VPN at the same time, each network sends it settings: an address, a gateway, a list of DNS servers. Some of those settings fit one network only, but the computer keeps them in a single global list. This RFC describes what goes wrong as a result, and what kinds of choices have to be made.

sections.title: Provisioning Domains and the MIF Node
sections.content:
Two terms carry most of the meaning. An administrative domain is a group of hosts, routers and networks operated and managed by a single organization. A provisioning domain is a set of consistent configuration information, such as a default router, network prefixes and DNS, together with the corresponding interface. One administrative domain may have multiple provisioning domains, and successful attachment to a provisioning domain means the terminal attaches to the corresponding interface with appropriate configuration information.

A MIF node has a specific set of characteristics. It is an IPv4- and/or IPv6-compliant node. It is configured with more than one IP address, excluding loopback and link-local addresses. It can attach to more than one provisioning domain as presented to the IP stack. The interfaces may be virtual or physical. Configuration objects come from one or more administrative domains. The IP addresses may be from the same or different address families. Communications using these addresses may happen simultaneously and independently. Some communications using them are possible on all the provisioning domains, while others are possible only on a smaller set of the provisioning domains. The node may forward packets between its interfaces, but that is not taken into account in the definition and is out of scope for this document.

When a protocol keyword such as IP, PPP or DHCP appears in the document without a reference to a specific IP version, it means both IPv4 and IPv6. A specific keyword such as DHCPv4 or DHCPv6 means that version only.
sections.plainLanguage: A provisioning domain is one network's worth of settings plus the interface they arrived on. An administrative domain is the organisation that runs the network. The RFC then lists what makes a node a multiple-interface node: more than one real IP address, more than one of these domains attached at the same time, and traffic that may run over them all at once.

sections.title: Related Work and Existing Practice
sections.content:
The RFC places several existing mechanisms outside its scope. Network discovery and selection on lower layers, and interoperability with services such as IEEE 802.21, which aims at facilitating handover between heterogeneous networks, are out of scope. So are mechanisms that share a single IP address over multiple interfaces, because from the IP stack's point of view there is then only a single interface and a single IP address, and link aggregation done under IP where a single interface is shown to the IP stack.

Several specifications already address parts of the problem. RFC 1122 describes the multihomed node as if it has multiple IP addresses, and defines two host models. Under the strong host model, a multihomed host is a set of logical hosts within the same physical host, and a packet must be sent on an interface that corresponds to the source address of that packet. Under the weak host model, the host has some embedded gateway functionality and can send and receive packets on any interface. The route for an outgoing datagram is computed differently under each: the strong model uses the source IP address, the destination IP address and the Differentiated Services Code Point, while the weak model does not use the source IP address at all.

IPv6 nodes must implement default address selection as defined in RFC 3484, which relies on a node-scoped policy table, and issues with multiple prefixes on the same link were reported in RFC 5220 and RFC 5221. Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) tests candidate IP addresses and ports for peer-to-peer connectivity, but it does not solve the case where incompatible configuration objects are received on different interfaces. Some application protocols refer peers to addresses, port numbers and transports for further exchanges, and those referrals have to be consistent with the provisioning domain in use.

There is no standard method for selecting a provisioning domain, though some recommendations exist for the narrower interface selection problem, using user preferences, network operator policies, radio link quality, network resource considerations such as available Quality of Service and an IP connectivity check, and the application's own QoS requirements. Some implementations, especially in the mobile world, rely on a higher-level session manager, also called a connection manager, to select the interface or the provisioning domain on behalf of applications and to resolve conflicting policies. The generic architecture of a session manager and its API are not standardized, so behaviour may differ between operating systems and platforms. Narrower APIs do exist: RFC 3542 lets an application specify the interface or source IP address with a bind() operation or the IPV6_PKTINFO socket option, RFC 5014 lets an application influence default address selection by stating which source address attributes it prefers, and RFC 6316 gives applications access to the multihoming shim layer for advanced locator management.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists what is already solved and what is deliberately left out. Picking which network to use has no standard method, so implementations often add a session manager, a piece of software that chooses the interface for the applications. Those session managers are not standardised, so two devices can behave differently in the same situation.

sections.title: The Issues a Multihomed Node Runs Into
sections.content:
Section 4 lists the issues. The example situations are a node with one interface on the Internet and another on a corporate private network, possibly through a VPN, and a node with one interface on WiFi and another on a 3G access network with specific services.

DNS resolution. Consider a node M1 with an active interface I1 on a network N1 whose primary DNS server S1 serves a private namespace, and an active interface I2 on a network N2 whose primary DNS server is S2. If the stack's routing table sends the query for a name in S1's private namespace out of I2, S1 is never reached and the name does not resolve. If the node keeps only one set of DNS server addresses, say S2's, the query gets NXDOMAIN from S2, and the reverse lookup fails as well. If S2 does answer, the address it returns need not be the one S1 would have given, so the application tries to connect to the wrong destination node or the wrong interface, which may imply security issues or a lack of service. If both networks use overlapping private address space, traffic may be sent using the wrong interface. If a name resolved to an address that was only locally valid on N1 and the node later moves to N2, connection setup fails, and a name that returned NXDOMAIN on N1 should not be assumed to be nonexistent on N2. A synthesized AAAA record learned from a network using protocol translators and DNS64 is guaranteed valid only on the network from which it was learned.

Networks that require the user to authenticate on a captive web portal add two more cases. Before the user authenticates, the portal's DNS server answers every A or AAAA query with the IP address of the portal, to redirect browsers to an access control page. If the node queries S2 instead, S2 gives the correct address but the node then tries to reach it through I1, so the connection fails, or it succeeds and bypasses the security policy on N1. If the node queries S1, it gets the portal address, and the application either fails to connect or reaches the portal instead of the intended destination.

Node routing. A node with a single default route through N1 never reaches a destination reachable only through N2. With one default route per network, the node uses the first one even when the other path has better characteristics such as round-trip time, least cost or bandwidth, so the destination is reached but the service is worse than it could be. With a specific route for a prefix that is used in both networks and a default route to the other network, the most specific route wins, packets leave through the wrong interface and never reach the target. A node usually has a node-scoped routing table, so if each provisioning domain pushes routing policies to it, conflicts arise with no easy way to merge them. Some source addresses are not valid on some interfaces, and if the source address is chosen wrongly, packets may be filtered by source address filtering and the reply packets never come back.

Conflicting policies. Address selection policies are often specific to a network. If two networks each send an update, the stack merges them, and the merged policy may choose a source address from N1 while packets are sent to N2, so the return packet is lost. Each connected domain may push its own routing policy, and again there is no easy way to reconcile them. A network-supplied access selection policy may conflict with the local user or operating system policy; if the network's policy is ignored, packets may be sent to an access network with poor communication quality.

Session management. An interface can be configured and active while Internet connectivity is still unavailable, because the network requires web-based authentication or because Layer 2 is so poor that no Layer 3 traffic can succeed. The session manager should be able to perform IP connectivity checks before selecting an interface. When a new network appears and is selected because of better communication quality, an existing TCP session may break, because with no specific route in place and the weak host model the connection breaks as the next hop changes; the node should try to reconnect over the new network, and in some situations it may be preferable to maintain current sessions on the old network while new sessions start on the new one. Even a node with a single interface connected to more than one network runs into the same problems, and may need different source addresses, default gateways and DNS servers per network.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists the failures in detail. The recurring shape is this: the node sends a query, an address or a packet out of the wrong interface, because the setting that would have told it which interface to use was stored as a single global value. The result is a name that does not resolve, an address that is wrong for this network, or a session that breaks when the network changes.

sections.title: Underlying Problems and Causes
sections.content:
Section 5 groups the causes into five categories. Configuration: configuration objects such as DNS and NTP servers are node-scoped, so the IP stack cannot keep the mapping between a piece of configuration and the domain it came from; the same objects received from several domains may overwrite each other; and host implementations usually do not keep separate network configurations per provisioning domain. DNS resolution: some names can only be resolved by the right server, yet a query may go out of the wrong interface because server addresses are node-scoped, and a DNS answer may be valid only on the domain it came from, which applications cannot tell.

Routing: routing information may be specific to each interface while routing tables are node-scoped; implementations do not take the Differentiated Services Code Point or path characteristics into account in the routing table; even when they do, the node has no way to merge or reconcile the preferences of different domains; and where the user and the network operator both supply selection policies, there is no way to reconcile them either. Address selection: default address selection policies may be domain-specific while the mechanism is node-scoped; some source addresses are invalid on some interfaces or on some default routers, and current implementations do not let the routing table account for the source address; and applications cannot specify a source address or an address selection policy because no advanced API supports it.

Session management and APIs: session managers exist but are not standardized and behave differently across operating systems and platforms; they rely on the link layer for information that the link layer may not provide; two session managers on the same node can solve the same problem in contradictory ways, with one preferring user policy and another preferring mobile operator policy; under the weak host model a route change can break an ongoing TCP session, which is why the strong host model should be used when TCP sessions should be bound to an interface; policies from different actors may conflict and need reconciling at the host level; and an interface may be configured while Internet connectivity is unavailable, so an IP connectivity check should be performed before an interface is selected.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC reduces all of this to five causes: settings kept globally instead of per network, names resolved by the wrong server, routes that are not tied to an interface, address choices that ignore the interface, and session managers that are not standardised.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The problems discussed in this document have security implications. Packets sent on the wrong interface might leak confidential information. Configuration parameters from one provisioning domain could cause a denial of service on another provisioning domain, for example through DNS issues. The undetermined behaviour of IP stacks in the multihomed context brings additional threats, because an interface on a multihomed node might be used to conduct attacks targeted at the networks connected by the other interfaces, and corrupted provisioning domain selection policy may induce a node to make decisions that cause certain traffic to be forwarded to the attacker.

Additional security concerns are raised by possible future mechanisms that provide additional information to the node so that it can make a more intelligent decision with regards to the issues discussed in this document. Such future mechanisms may themselves be vulnerable and may not be easy to protect in the general case.
sections.plainLanguage: Getting the interface wrong is a security problem, not only a convenience one: traffic may leak onto the wrong network, one network's settings may break another's service, and a device with several interfaces can be used to reach networks it should not. Any future help for the node has to be protected too.
